nodes.title: AiSOC v23.3.0 — two security advisories fixed and published same-day, plus Cisco Secure Endpoint
nodes.body:
**AiSOC v23.3.0 is out** — [release](https://github.com/beenuar/AiSOC/releases/tag/v23.3.0) · [changelog](https://github.com/beenuar/AiSOC/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md)

This one is about response time: **two community-reported security advisories were triaged, reproduced, fixed, released and published — with the reporters credited — within a day of landing in the queue.** If you report a vulnerability to this project, this is the turnaround we aim for.

## Security, same day

- **[GHSA-qfvv-rf5p-6h69](https://github.com/beenuar/AiSOC/security/advisories/GHSA-qfvv-rf5p-6h69)** (high) — reported by **1ceS1amese** with a working PoC. Fusion's synchronous `POST /process` trusted the request body's `tenant_id`, so any logged-in user could inject alerts into another tenant's live dedup/correlation/risk state — and because deduplication registered the injected fingerprint under the victim tenant, their *real* alerts could be silently absorbed as duplicates. The tenant now comes from the credential, submission requires a role holding `alerts:write` (mirrored from the API's role table and pinned by a drift test), and the same contract covers every sibling write route in the service.
- **[GHSA-qf6m-hgwv-65f9](https://github.com/beenuar/AiSOC/security/advisories/GHSA-qf6m-hgwv-65f9)** (medium) — reported by **naroSEC** with a precise version history. The enrichment service authenticated nobody, two console rewrites made it same-origin reachable, and its rate limiter was keyed on a body field anyone could rotate — an anonymous client could spend your VirusTotal/AbuseIPDB/GreyNoise quota. The service now authenticates every caller (console session or service token + declared tenant, failing closed when unconfigured), keys its limiter and cache on the authenticated tenant, and the dead console rewrites are gone.

Both advisories name **23.3.0** as the patched version. Upgrading is `make upgrade` (never plain `up` — it runs the preflight, the pre-upgrade dump and the strict migration chain for you).

## New integration: Cisco Secure Endpoint

The catalogue's 93rd connector, contributed by **@officialasishkumar** ([#1842](https://github.com/beenuar/AiSOC/pull/1842), from the [connector wishlist](https://github.com/beenuar/AiSOC/issues/356)): Cisco Secure Endpoint (formerly AMP for Endpoints) detections through the v1 events API — the same feed Cisco's own SIEM integrations read. The region is a closed choice of Cisco's three clouds, so your API key can only ever reach a Cisco host; the poll window is read to the end at the documented 500-event page maximum; operational noise (policy updates, scans, installs) stays out of your alert queue; and Cisco's four severities map one-to-one, with `Critical` kept `critical`.

And it didn't stop at the tag: the **Huntress** connector (same contributor) and a **Neo4j concurrency fix** for incident context (**@43n51c** — four of five context dimensions were silently dropping on real escalations) merged right behind the release, with a tracing-noise fix for three services close behind. All of it rides the next release.

## The numbers

**2 defects fixed in this release, 22 across it and the two before** (2 here, 11 in v23.2.0, 9 in v23.1.0 — counting distinct product or CI defects named in each release's Fixed and Security sections, dependency advisories excluded). 63 of 64 release-workflow jobs green on the first run, and the one transient failure (an upstream OIDC 504 during SBOM signing) re-ran to green with every image verified at the registry: multi-arch (amd64+arm64) at `v23.3.0`, chart `7.22.0`.

Thanks to this release's reporters and contributors: **1ceS1amese**, **naroSEC**, **@officialasishkumar**, **@43n51c**.

nodes.title: [RFC-0003] Payments, Compliance and Runtime Boundaries
nodes.body:
## RFC-0003: Payments, Compliance and Runtime Boundaries

**Status:** Draft  
**Date:** 2026-07-14  
**Depends on:** [RFC-0001](https://github.com/orgs/mavulahq/discussions/1) and [RFC-0002](https://github.com/orgs/mavulahq/discussions/4)

## Resumo

Esta RFC propõe as fronteiras de runtime para pagamentos e compliance e define a introdução controlada de Java e Go na plataforma MAVULA.

A proposta separa três tipos de workload:

- integração concorrente e stateless com providers em Go;
- estado transacional, reconciliação e workflows duráveis de pagamentos em Java;
- alertas, casos, decisões e reporting de compliance em Java.

A escolha das linguagens não é baseada em preferência individual. Performance, segurança, consistência transacional, interoperabilidade, maturidade do ecossistema e capacidade de operação da equipa são avaliadas em conjunto.

Esta discussão permanece Draft e não autoriza implementação, migração, criação de repositórios ou alteração do roadmap antes do encerramento dos gates definidos nesta RFC.

## Decisões propostas

- `payment-connectors` será um novo módulo Go e a fronteira técnica com providers externos.
- `settlements` permanece owner de Payments e será migrado gradualmente de TypeScript para Java.
- `compliance` será um novo bounded context Java.
- `ledger-core` permanece a única fonte da verdade financeira.
- `identity-access` continua owner de roles, permissions e designações institucionais.
- `workbench` continua owner de schedules, jobs, retries e DLQ, mas deixa de executar o package TypeScript de `settlements` após o cutover.
- Nenhum connector ou módulo de compliance pode escrever diretamente nos stores de `ledger-core`, `settlements` ou `identity-access`.

## Módulos e runtimes

### `payment-connectors`

Novo repositório Go responsável por:

- endpoints de webhook específicos por provider;
- verificação de assinatura e replay protection;
- timeouts, retries e circuit breaking de chamadas externas;
- isolamento de credenciais e configuração de providers;
- tradução entre protocolos externos e contratos canónicos MAVULA;
- receipts operacionais para callbacks e requests externos.

O módulo não possui estado de settlement, não decide transições de pagamento e não publica `payments.settlement_completed`.

Baseline proposta:

- Go 1.26.x, inicialmente 1.26.5, revisto no gate de implementação;
- módulo `github.com/mavulahq/payment-connectors`;
- `net/http`, PostgreSQL para receipts e OpenTelemetry;
- sandbox determinístico, seguido por M-Pesa e e-Mola.

### `settlements`

O repositório e o nome `settlements` são preservados. O runtime TypeScript será substituído gradualmente por um serviço Java responsável por:

- processos e estados de pagamento;
- idempotência por tenant e operation key;
- webhook receipts e provider references;
- reconciliação, disputas e tratamento de exceções;
- Outbox de domínio;
- produção exclusiva de `payments.settlement_completed`;
- APIs internas para iniciação, consulta, callbacks normalizados e reconciliação.

Baseline proposta:

- Java 25 LTS;
- Spring Boot 4.1.x;
- Maven Wrapper;
- PostgreSQL e Flyway;
- Spring Batch para reconciliação restartable e workloads batch.

### `compliance`

Novo bounded context Java responsável por:

- alertas de monitorização;
- casos e investigações;
- decisões AML/BC/FT/FP;
- referências de evidência e cadeia de custódia;
- pedidos de hold, release ou reject aos owners financeiros;
- artefactos e entregas regulatórias;
- reporting e interoperabilidade goAML numa fatia posterior.

Baseline proposta:

- Java 25 LTS;
- Spring Boot 4.1.x;
- Maven Wrapper;
- PostgreSQL, Flyway e RLS;
- Spring Security Resource Server;
- Spring Batch reservado para reporting e exports.

## Camadas

1. **Identity and authorisation:** `identity-access` emite claims institucionais e permissions efetivas.
2. **Provider edge:** `payment-connectors` autentica e traduz tráfego externo.
3. **Payment domain:** `settlements` mantém o processo e decide transições.
4. **Automation:** `workbench` executa jobs, schedules, retries e DLQ.
5. **Financial core:** `ledger-core` aplica invariantes financeiras e ledger posting.
6. **Compliance domain:** `compliance` gere alertas, casos, decisões e pedidos de controlo.
7. **Operator surfaces:** `console` e `developer-docs` consomem apenas APIs aprovadas.
8. **Platform operations:** `operations` provisiona PostgreSQL, secrets, mTLS, observabilidade e deployments.

## Fluxo de pagamentos

1. `workbench` ou um cliente interno submete uma instrução idempotente a `settlements`.
2. `settlements` cria o processo durável antes de solicitar qualquer efeito externo.
3. `settlements` chama `payment-connectors` através de API interna autenticada.
4. O connector comunica com o provider e devolve a referência técnica.
5. O provider envia o webhook para um endpoint específico do connector.
6. O connector deriva tenant e provider da configuração do endpoint, valida assinatura e replay e persiste o receipt antes do acknowledgement.
7. O callback normalizado é entregue a `settlements`.
8. `settlements` decide a transição, reconcilia e grava a Outbox.
9. `settlements` publica `payments.settlement_completed`.
10. `ledger-core` consome o evento através de Inbox idempotente, sem permitir escrita direta pelo connector.

## Fluxo de compliance

1. `compliance` consome factos financeiros e de settlement através de Inbox idempotente.
2. Regras de monitorização podem abrir um alerta.
3. Um `compliance_officer` assume o caso, associa evidências e regista uma decisão.
4. Quando necessário, compliance cria um pedido idempotente de hold, release ou reject.
5. O owner financeiro aceita, rejeita ou aplica o controlo e devolve um resultado auditável.
6. Compliance regista o resultado sem escrever diretamente no store do owner.
7. A primeira fatia não cria dependência síncrona obrigatória de compliance para todas as transações.

## Compliance officer e OCOS

`compliance_officer` permanece uma role institucional funcional e não recebe `finance.write` nem `finance.approve`.

Permissions propostas:

- `compliance.alert.read`
- `compliance.case.manage`
- `compliance.decision.record`
- `compliance.control.request`
- `compliance.report.submit`

`compliance.report.submit` exige uma designação OCOS institucional válida, separada da role. A designação identifica operador, instituição, vigência, estado e referência de registo.

Institution administrators e auditors não recebem acesso automático a casos AML. O acesso deve seguir need-to-know, preservar confidencialidade e impedir divulgação indevida.

## Contratos públicos e internos

Contratos canónicos serão language-neutral e versionados por JSON Schema e OpenAPI:

- `ProviderPaymentCommand`
- `ProviderPaymentResult`
- `ProviderWebhookEnvelope`
- `ProviderReconciliationRecord`
- `SettlementProcess`
- `SettlementStatus`
- `ComplianceAlert`
- `ComplianceCase`
- `ComplianceDecision`
- `ComplianceControlRequest`
- `RegulatoryReport`

Todos incluem tenant, instituição, correlation id, causation id e idempotency key quando aplicável.

Nenhum contrato transporta PAN, segredos de provider ou informação AML em metadata livre.

Eventos inicialmente propostos:

- `compliance.alert_opened`
- `compliance.decision_recorded`
- `compliance.report_submitted`

Callbacks de provider e pedidos de controlo são contratos internos, não eventos públicos de domínio. Nenhum novo evento será ativado sem schema, producer, consumer, Outbox/Inbox, observabilidade e testes.

## Migração de settlements

A migração não será uma reescrita direta nem permitirá dois writers de produção simultâneos.

1. Congelar novas alterações estruturais no runtime TypeScript durante a migração.
2. Extrair contratos canónicos e characterization tests do comportamento atual.
3. Implementar o serviço Java contra PostgreSQL isolado e migrations Flyway equivalentes.
4. Executar testes de paridade TypeScript/Java para estados, idempotência, webhooks, reconciliação e Outbox.
5. Executar shadow processing em schema separado, com calls a providers e publicação de Outbox desativadas.
6. No cutover, drenar queues e Outbox, criar backup, desativar o runtime TypeScript e apontar `workbench` para a API Java.
7. Manter o runtime TypeScript disponível para rollback durante uma release, sem aceitar novas alterações de schema.
8. Remover a dependência `@mavula/settlements` do `workbench` após estabilização.

## Gates de implementação

A implementação começa apenas depois da RFC-0002 entregar:

- account lifecycle e correções controladas;
- reversões e maker-checker;
- `AuditTrailEvent.stage`;
- idempotency receipts duráveis;
- contratos regulatórios mínimos;
- contratos públicos estáveis para integração.

## Ordem de entrega

1. Contratos language-neutral e CI Java/Go.
2. Fundação Java de `settlements` e testes de paridade.
3. Sandbox Go e adapter M-Pesa.
4. Adapter e-Mola e reconciliação.
5. Cutover controlado de `settlements`.
6. Designação OCOS e permissions granulares.
7. Alertas e case management em `compliance`.
8. Decisões e pedidos de controlo.
9. Reporting regulatório e interoperabilidade goAML.

## Segurança e observabilidade

- Client Credentials com `private_key_jwt` e mTLS entre serviços.
- RLS e roles PostgreSQL sem BYPASSRLS.
- Secrets apenas através de `operations` e stores apropriados.
- Logs sem payloads financeiros, credenciais ou conteúdo AML sensível.
- Métricas de assinatura inválida, replay, timeout, retries, reconciliação, alertas, casos e control requests.
- Traces preservam correlation id sem expor dados restritos.
- Avaliação PCI formal antes de qualquer suporte a dados de cartão.

## Validação

- Contract tests equivalentes em TypeScript, Java e Go.
- Paridade integral entre runtimes antes do cutover.
- Webhooks duplicados, inválidos, reproduzidos ou fora de ordem não alteram processos.
- Provider outages não geram cobranças ou transições duplicadas.
- Reconciliação compara provider, settlement e ledger sem escrita cross-context.
- RLS impede acesso cross-tenant em conexões reutilizadas.
- `compliance_officer` não aprova operações financeiras nem submete reportes sem designação OCOS.
- Pedidos de controlo são idempotentes e auditáveis.
- CI executa Maven tests, integration tests, `go test`, `go vet`, `govulncheck`, dependency scanning, migrations e guardian checks.

## Licenciamento

- `settlements`, `compliance` e o framework aberto de `payment-connectors`: `AGPL-3.0-only`.
- Connectors proprietários e compliance packs exigem decisão de governança e licença separada.
- Nomes, marcas e domínios MAVULA permanecem reservados.

## Fora do escopo

- Event Sourcing financeiro.
- Escrita direta de connectors ou compliance no ledger.
- Migração imediata antes dos gates da RFC-0002.
- Implementação de `console`, mobile ou intelligence.
- Certificação jurídica, regulatória ou PCI através desta RFC.

## Fontes técnicas e regulatórias

- [Go release history](https://go.dev/doc/devel/release)
- [Oracle Java SE Support Roadmap](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/java-se-support-roadmap.html)
- [Spring Boot system requirements](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/system-requirements.html)
- [Spring Batch reference](https://docs.spring.io/spring-batch/reference/index.html)
- [Banco de Moçambique, Relatório de Avaliação Sectorial 2025](https://www.bancomoc.mz/media/kckjq0ty/relato-rio-de-avaliac-a-o-sectorial-2025.pdf)
- [Banco de Moçambique, cadastro de OCOS](https://www.bancomoc.mz/media/o10ncg5d/comunicado-cadastro-de-oficiais-de-comunica%C3%A7%C3%A3o-de-opera%C3%A7%C3%B5es-suspeitas.pdf)
- [PCI SSC, tokenisation and PCI scope](https://www.pcisecuritystandards.org/faqs/1326/)

Esta definição é técnica, permanece sujeita a revisão pública e não substitui validação formal com instituições licenciadas, providers, Banco de Moçambique, GIFiM ou assessoria jurídica e PCI competente.

nodes.title: Enterprise MCP Gateway – Secretless Agent Identity, Token Exchange and Downstream Authorization
nodes.body:
Hi,

We're evaluating LiteLLM as a central enterprise MCP gateway and comparing it with AWS AgentCore Gateway.

Our agents run in AWS, across multiple accounts, and need access to tools such as ServiceNow, Elastic, and Azure DevOps.

The goal is to centralize authentication and authorization without giving agents direct credentials or permissions to downstream tools.

The flow we're aiming for:

1. An AWS-hosted agent authenticates to the gateway using its workload identity, without stored secrets.
2. The gateway identifies the specific agent and enforces which tools it can access.
3. When calling a tool, the gateway obtains a downstream access token representing that agent, ideally using Microsoft Entra Agent Identity.
4. For user-delegated scenarios, the gateway should also support OBO, preserving both the user and agent context.
5. Agents should only be authorized to access the gateway, not downstream services directly.

We're looking for a solution that can scale to many agents, with centralized policies, auditing, and minimal custom authentication code.

A few questions:

- Does LiteLLM's current MCP OAuth/token exchange support this architecture, particularly for headless AWS agents?
- Can LiteLLM obtain downstream tokens for distinct Entra Agent Identities without storing per-agent client secrets?
- How is agent identity preserved and enforced across the gateway and downstream services, including OBO scenarios?
- Can the gateway dynamically map an authenticated agent to its downstream identity and permissions?
- Would another identity approach or provider be better suited for this architecture than Entra Agent Identity?
- Which parts are supported natively today, and which require a custom identity broker or additional integration?

I'd also be interested in hearing from anyone running a similar architecture in production, particularly if you've evaluated LiteLLM against AgentCore Gateway.

Thanks!

nodes.title: Feature: Rust Based MongoDB Read Connector for Daft
nodes.body:
## Feature Summary

Add a Rust based `daft.read_mongodb()` connector that reads MongoDB collections into Daft DataFrames with explicit schema, server-side filter and projection pushdown, and optional distributed range reads. The connector is designed for operational MongoDB workloads: it does not sample or infer schema during planning, and it exposes knobs such as `hint`, `max_time_ms`, and user-provided `partition_ranges` to keep reads bounded and index-friendly. BSON values are converted into the user-provided Daft schema at execution time, with support for nested structs and lists.

## Example Usage

```python
import datetime
import daft

schema = {
    "_id": daft.DataType.string(),
    "tenant_id": daft.DataType.string(),
    "created_at": daft.DataType.timestamp("ms"),
    "amount": daft.DataType.float64(),
    "profile": daft.DataType.struct(
        {
            "name": daft.DataType.string(),
            "score": daft.DataType.int64(),
        }
    ),
    "tags": daft.DataType.list(daft.DataType.string()),
}

# Basic read with server-side filter and projection
df = daft.read_mongodb(
    uri="mongodb://localhost:27017/?readPreference=secondaryPreferred",
    database="app",
    collection="orders",
    schema=schema,
    filter={"status": "paid"},
    projection={"_id": 1, "tenant_id": 1, "created_at": 1, "amount": 1, "profile": 1, "tags": 1},
    hint={"status": 1, "created_at": 1},
    max_time_ms=30_000,
    batch_size=1000,
)

# Push additional Daft predicates and projections into MongoDB when supported
result = (
    df.where(daft.col("amount") >= 100)
    .select("tenant_id", "amount", "profile")
)

# Distributed reads across Ray workers using explicit half-open partition ranges
utc = datetime.timezone.utc
df_distributed = daft.read_mongodb(
    uri="mongodb://localhost:27017",
    database="app",
    collection="orders",
    schema=schema,
    filter={"status": "paid"},
    partition_field="created_at",  # may be omitted from output schema
    partition_ranges=[
        (datetime.datetime(2024, 1, 1, tzinfo=utc), datetime.datetime(2024, 2, 1, tzinfo=utc)),
        (datetime.datetime(2024, 2, 1, tzinfo=utc), datetime.datetime(2024, 3, 1, tzinfo=utc)),
        (datetime.datetime(2024, 3, 1, tzinfo=utc), datetime.datetime(2024, 4, 1, tzinfo=utc)),
    ],
    hint={"created_at": 1},
)

# ObjectId and other non-JSON BSON values via MongoDB Extended JSON
df_by_id = daft.read_mongodb(
    uri="mongodb://localhost:27017",
    database="app",
    collection="orders",
    schema=schema,
    filter={"_id": {"$oid": "000000000000000000000000"}},
)
```

## Corner-case Behavior

### Schema and BSON conversion

- **Explicit schema required:** Planning does not inspect the collection. Users must provide the expected Daft schema up front.
- **Missing fields / BSON null:** Read as Daft nulls.
- **Nested documents and arrays:** Supported when declared in the schema (e.g. `struct`, `list`).
- **Type coercion:** BSON values are converted to the provided Daft types at execution time; values that cannot be converted should surface as execution errors rather than silently changing semantics.

### Filters and predicate pushdown

- **User `filter` + Daft `where`:** Supported MongoDB predicates are merged into a single server-side filter document.
- **Supported pushed predicates:** Column comparisons (`==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`), `between`, `is_in` with literals, `is_null`, `not_null`, and conjunctions of supported predicates.
- **Unsupported predicates:** Expressions involving casts, functions, arithmetic, `not`, or unsupported operators are not pushed to MongoDB.
- **Strict filter pushdown mode:** When `daft.context.set_planning_config(enable_strict_filter_pushdown=True)` is enabled, unsupported predicates remain above the scan. Without strict mode, planning fails if a pushed filter cannot be fully represented in MongoDB.
- **`!=` semantics:** Pushed as a null-safe MongoDB filter using `$exists`, `$ne: null`, and `$ne: <value>`.
- **Extended JSON in filters:** `$oid`, `$numberLong`, `$numberInt`, `$numberDouble`, `$date`, and canonical `$binary` are accepted; malformed or non-canonical extended JSON is rejected at planning time.

### Projection pushdown

- **Daft `select` pushdown:** Selected columns are pushed into the MongoDB projection when possible.
- **Default `_id` behavior:** If `_id` is not in the Daft schema, MongoDB's default `_id` field is excluded from the server projection unless the user projection explicitly includes it.
- **Projection validation:** MongoDB's inclusion/exclusion rules are enforced; mixing inclusion and exclusion fields (except `_id`) is rejected at planning time.

### Distributed reads and partitioning

- **`partition_ranges` omitted:** A single scan task is created. No hidden metadata query is issued to infer collection bounds.
- **`partition_ranges` provided:** `partition_field` is required. One MongoDB scan task is created per half-open `(lower, upper)` range.
- **Unbounded ranges:** `None` on the lower or upper bound means unbounded on that side.
- **Invalid ranges:** Empty or reversed ranges (`lower >= upper`) are rejected at planning time.
- **Partition field outside schema:** Allowed when the field is only used to bound MongoDB queries and should not appear in the output DataFrame.
- **Range pruning:** When filters constrain `partition_field` with comparable values (`$eq`, `$in`, `$gt`, `$gte`, `$lt`, `$lte`, and supported `$and` / `$or` shapes), scan tasks for non-overlapping ranges are skipped.
- **Conservative pruning:** If a filter contains opaque values or partially unsupported operators on `partition_field` (e.g. `$in` with nested documents, mixed `$or` branches), all partition ranges are retained to avoid dropping data.
- **Impossible filters:** Contradictory constraints (e.g. `{"value": {"$gte": 20, "$lt": 10}}` or `{"value": {"$in": []}}`) result in zero scan tasks.

### Limits, batching, and operational safety

- **`limit` pushdown:** Applied to MongoDB only when a single scan task remains after partitioning/pruning. For multiple scan tasks, per-task limits are not pushed and Daft applies the limit after the scan.
- **`max_time_ms`:** Bounds each server-side `find` operation.
- **`hint`:** Accepts either an index key document or an index name string.
- **`batch_size`:** Controls MongoDB cursor batch size and acts as a Daft task batch hint.
- **Connection reuse:** MongoDB clients are cached per URI within a process.

### Out of scope for initial proposal

- **Automatic schema inference:** Intentionally omitted to avoid expensive collection scans during planning.
- **Automatic partition discovery:** Users must provide explicit `partition_ranges` for distributed reads.

This discussion proposes adding Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) `ActiveDirectoryServicePrincipal` authentication as a **non-breaking** option for the MSSQL source connector, leveraging the JDBC driver's native support.

### Related Issues

- [#20866](https://github.com/airbytehq/airbyte/issues/20866) — "Source MSSQL - Failed to load MSAL4J Java library for performing ActiveDirectoryPassword authentication" (frozen)
- [Community PR #61547](https://github.com/airbytehq/airbyte/pull/61547) — Previous community attempt (closed during CDK migration)

### Prior Art (Closed PR)
A reference implementation was developed in [PR #74904](https://github.com/airbytehq/airbyte/pull/74904) (now closed) on branch `devin/1773700827-mssql-entra-id-auth`. The code changes are preserved there for reference.

---

## Motivation

Multiple users across issues #9557 and #20866 have stated that the lack of Entra ID / non-SQL-password authentication is a **dealbreaker** for their organizations:

> *"Lack of this feature disqualifies Airbyte as a candidate for our organization (big Danish governmental organization)."*

> *"For organizations heavy on MSSQL, it makes the entire Airbyte software kind of a non-starter."*

Many enterprises require Entra ID authentication for Azure SQL Database / Azure Synapse Analytics and cannot use SQL Server authentication for security compliance reasons.

---

## Proposed Approach

### Leverage JDBC Driver's Native Support

The MSSQL JDBC driver (`mssql-jdbc:12.10.1`) already supports Entra ID authentication natively via the `authentication` connection property. The `azure-identity:1.15.3` dependency is **already present** in the connector's `build.gradle`. No new dependencies are needed.

### Non-Breaking Design

Add an **optional** `authentication` oneOf selector to the connector spec (following the existing `EncryptionSpecification` sealed interface pattern):

- **`sql_password`** (default) — username + password (current behavior, fully backward compatible)
- **`active_directory_service_principal`** (new) — tenant_id + client_id + client_secret

When no `authentication` block is present in the config, the connector falls back to top-level `username`/`password` fields — **zero disruption to existing connections**.

### JDBC Property Mapping

| Auth Method | JDBC Properties Set |
|---|---|
| SQL Password (current) | `user` = username, `password` = password |
| Service Principal (new) | `user` = client_id, `password` = client_secret, `authentication` = `ActiveDirectoryServicePrincipal`, `tenantId` = tenant_id |

### Implementation Details

The reference implementation (branch `devin/1773700827-mssql-entra-id-auth`) touches three files:

1. **`MsSqlServerSourceConfigurationSpecification.kt`**
   - Makes `username`/`password` fields nullable (from `lateinit var` to `var String? = null`)
   - Adds `AuthenticationSpecification` sealed interface with `SqlPasswordAuthentication` and `ActiveDirectoryServicePrincipalAuthentication` variants
   - Adds `@JsonSetter`/`@JsonGetter` methods for the optional `authentication` block
   - Adds `MicronautPropertiesFriendlyAuthenticationSpecification` for Micronaut DI compatibility

2. **`MsSqlServerSourceConfiguration.kt`**
   - Updates the factory to check for `authenticationJson` and set JDBC properties accordingly
   - Falls back to top-level `username`/`password` when no auth block is present

3. **`MsSqlServerSourceConfigurationSpecificationTest.kt`**
   - Adds tests for backward compatibility, SQL password auth block, and service principal auth block

### Why Not OAuth/Consent Flow?

The Azure Blob Storage connector uses a platform-level OAuth consent flow (`MicrosoftAzureBlobStorageOAuthFlow.kt` in `airbyte-platform-internal`). This approach was evaluated but is **not recommended** for MSSQL because:
- The JDBC driver handles token acquisition internally — manually managing tokens would fight the driver's architecture
- It would require changes in both the connector repo AND `airbyte-platform-internal`
- Service Principal auth is the enterprise standard for machine-to-machine workloads like data pipelines
- No other JDBC-based Airbyte connector uses a platform-side OAuth consent flow

### Future Extensions

Phase 2 could add:
- `ActiveDirectoryDefault` — uses `DefaultAzureCredential` (managed identity for Azure-hosted Airbyte)
- `ActiveDirectoryPassword` — Entra username + password (deprecated by Microsoft but still supported)
- User-delegated OAuth consent flow (if demand justifies the cross-repo complexity)

---

## Open Questions

1. **Version bump**: Should this be a patch bump (4.3.6) or minor bump (4.4.0)? The change is additive and non-breaking.
2. **SpotBugs**: The reference implementation triggered SpotBugs warnings due to nullable `username`/`password` fields. Need to add appropriate `@SuppressFBWarnings` annotations or restructure.
3. **JSON schema ordering**: The `authentication` field uses `"order":4`, which may collide with the existing `username` field. May need adjustment.
4. **Documentation**: What level of docs changes are needed? (connector docs, migration guide, etc.)

---

nodes.title: `stream_partition` in `AddFields` resolves to same value across all partitions
nodes.body:
I have a declarative connector (Connector Builder, CDK 7.17.1) with three streams:

1. auth — fetches per-tenant credentials from an external secrets API, outputs records each containing a pre-computed Basic Auth header
2. parent — uses `SubstreamPartitionRouter` with auth as `parent. partition_field: auth_header` + request_option injects the Authorization header per tenant. Works correctly — each tenant's data is fetched with the right credentials.
3. child — substream of parent. Needs each parent record's auth_header to authenticate detail requests for the correct tenant.

To pass `auth_header` from parent to child, I use `AddFields` on the parent stream to stamp each record:

```yaml
  - type: AddedFieldDefinition
    path:
      - auth_header
    value: "{{ stream_partition.extra_fields['auth_header'] }}"
```

The child then reads it via parent_key: `auth_header`.

**Problem**: The AddFields Jinja expression resolves to the same partition's value for every record across all partitions. All parent records end up with one tenant's auth header, so the child sends all requests with wrong credentials.

I've tried `stream_partition.<partition_field>`, `stream_partition.extra_fields['...']`, renaming fields to avoid collisions, and `concurrency_level: 1` — all produce the same result. Meanwhile, `request_option` and URL templates correctly resolve per-partition.

Is there a known issue with `stream_partition` inside `AddFields` in the concurrent code path? Or a different way to propagate partition data onto output records?

nodes.title: 🔌 Connecting Security Vendors (CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, Defender & More)
nodes.body:
# Connecting Security Vendors to SentryLog

SentryLog Enterprise includes connectors for major security platforms. Pull alerts, detections, and events directly into your unified log dashboard.

## Supported Vendors (Enterprise Tier)

| Vendor | Connector | Data Pulled |
|--------|-----------|-------------|
| **CrowdStrike Falcon** | REST API | Detections, incidents, host info |
| **SentinelOne** | REST API | Threats, activities, agent status |
| **Microsoft Defender** | Graph API | Alerts, incidents, device info |
| **Sophos Central** | REST API | Alerts, events, endpoint status |
| **Palo Alto Cortex XDR** | REST API | Incidents, alerts, endpoint data |
| **Generic REST** | Configurable | Any JSON API endpoint |

## Configuration

Add vendor connectors to your `config.yaml`:

### CrowdStrike Falcon
```yaml
security_vendors:
  crowdstrike:
    enabled: true
    client_id: "your-api-client-id"
    client_secret: "your-api-client-secret"
    base_url: "https://api.crowdstrike.com"
    poll_interval_seconds: 60
    severity_filter: "medium"    # minimum severity to import
```

### SentinelOne
```yaml
security_vendors:
  sentinelone:
    enabled: true
    api_token: "your-api-token"
    base_url: "https://your-tenant.sentinelone.net"
    poll_interval_seconds: 60
```

### Microsoft Defender
```yaml
security_vendors:
  defender:
    enabled: true
    tenant_id: "your-azure-tenant-id"
    client_id: "your-app-client-id"
    client_secret: "your-app-client-secret"
    poll_interval_seconds: 120
```

### Sophos Central
```yaml
security_vendors:
  sophos:
    enabled: true
    client_id: "your-partner-client-id"
    client_secret: "your-partner-client-secret"
    poll_interval_seconds: 60
```

### Palo Alto Cortex XDR
```yaml
security_vendors:
  cortex_xdr:
    enabled: true
    api_key: "your-api-key"
    api_key_id: "your-key-id"
    base_url: "https://api-yourfqdn.xdr.us.paloaltonetworks.com"
    poll_interval_seconds: 120
```

### Generic REST Connector
```yaml
security_vendors:
  custom_vendor:
    enabled: true
    type: generic_rest
    url: "https://api.example.com/v1/alerts"
    method: GET
    headers:
      Authorization: "Bearer your-token"
    poll_interval_seconds: 300
    json_path: "data.alerts"     # JSONPath to the alerts array
```

## How It Works

1. SentryLog polls each vendor API at the configured interval
2. New detections/alerts are normalized into SentryLog's unified schema
3. Events appear in the dashboard with vendor-specific icons and severity mapping
4. Correlation engine can match vendor alerts with syslog events from the same host

## Correlation Engine

When a security vendor reports a detection on a host, SentryLog can:
- Cross-reference with syslog events from that host's IP
- Highlight related network activity in the timeline
- Generate a unified incident view combining all data sources

## Tips

- 🔑 **Least privilege** — Create read-only API keys for each vendor
- 🕐 **Poll intervals** — 60s is good for most; increase for rate-limited APIs
- 📊 **Dashboards** — Each vendor gets its own widget on the security overview page
- 🔔 **Alerts** — Configure SentryLog to alert on high-severity vendor detections

Questions? Post below! 🍀

nodes.title: RFC: Apache IoTDB 2.x Table Model as a new time-series backend
nodes.body:
Hi ThingsBoard community,

I'm Zihan Dai ([@PDGGK](https://github.com/PDGGK)), a GSoC 2026 applicant working with the Apache IoTDB project. My background is in open-source contributions to Apache projects — I have merged PRs in IoTDB ([#17212](https://github.com/apache/iotdb/pull/17212)), Beam, ShardingSphere, Iceberg, and OpenCV, mostly focused on resource management and DAO-layer reliability.

My IoTDB mentor (Xuan Wang, @critas) suggested reaching out to the ThingsBoard community early, before writing production code, to make sure the design aligns with where ThingsBoard is headed.

---

## What this project is

This is a GSoC project to implement ThingsBoard telemetry persistence against **Apache IoTDB 2.x's Table Model** — a full rewrite of the existing tree-model plugin, not a patch on top of it.

The deliverable is a new backend activated by `database.ts.type=iotdb-table` that implements the three core interfaces:

- `TimeseriesDao` — write and query telemetry history
- `TimeseriesLatestDao` — latest-value reads for dashboards
- `AttributeDao` — entity attribute storage

The integration will initially live in the `apache/iotdb-extras` repository (alongside the existing Grafana connector), with the intent of submitting a PR to ThingsBoard once it is stable and tested.

---

## Why a rewrite, not a patch

The existing tree-model PR ([apache/iotdb#11476](https://github.com/apache/iotdb/pull/11476)) uses `SessionPool.insertRecord()` with path-based device addressing (`root.thingsboard.<entityId>`) and IoTDB-specific query syntax (`MAX_VALUE()`, `group by` with interval notation, `select last`).

IoTDB 2.x's Table Model is a fundamentally different API: data is written via `ITableSession.insert(Tablet)`, queries are standard SQL with typed TAG/FIELD columns, and aggregation uses `MAX()`, `date_bin()`, etc. There is no migration path from the tree-model code — it has to be rewritten from scratch.

---

## Schema design

**Telemetry table** — one table for all entities and all telemetry keys:

```sql
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS thingsboard;

CREATE TABLE telemetry (
    tenant_id   STRING  TAG,
    entity_type STRING  TAG,
    entity_id   STRING  TAG,
    key         STRING  TAG,
    bool_v      BOOLEAN FIELD,
    long_v      INT64   FIELD,
    double_v    DOUBLE  FIELD,
    str_v       TEXT    FIELD,
    json_v      TEXT    FIELD
) WITH (TTL=2592000000);
```

This maps directly to ThingsBoard's `TsKvEntry` structure. The TAG columns let us filter by entity and metric name using SQL `WHERE` clauses. Exactly one value column is non-null per row, matching `AbstractTsKvEntity`'s typed fields. IoTDB's built-in `time` column is the timestamp. Table-level TTL handles retention without application-side cleanup jobs.

**Attribute table** — separate from telemetry, no time dimension:

```sql
CREATE TABLE entity_attributes (
    tenant_id      STRING  TAG,
    entity_type    STRING  TAG,
    entity_id      STRING  TAG,
    attribute_type STRING  TAG,
    attribute_key  STRING  TAG,
    bool_v         BOOLEAN FIELD,
    long_v         INT64   FIELD,
    double_v       DOUBLE  FIELD,
    str_v          TEXT    FIELD,
    json_v         TEXT    FIELD,
    last_update_ts INT64   FIELD
) WITH (TTL=INFINITE);
```

The `attribute_type` TAG distinguishes CLIENT_SCOPE, SERVER_SCOPE, and SHARED_SCOPE. This uses the same multi-type value column pattern as the telemetry table for consistency, but with `TTL=INFINITE` since attributes are not time-series data.

---

## PoC

I have a working proof-of-concept that validates the session management, multi-type Tablet writes, SQL queries, and TTL configuration against a live IoTDB 2.x instance:

**https://github.com/PDGGK/thingsboard-iotdb-table-poc**

It is not production code — it is a design validation. The actual implementation will follow ThingsBoard's Spring `@ConditionalOnProperty` plugin pattern and submit as a series of incremental PRs.

---

## Questions for the ThingsBoard team

**1. DAO interface stability**
The implementation targets `TimeseriesDao`, `TimeseriesLatestDao`, and `AttributeDao` as they exist today. Are there known changes to these interfaces planned for upcoming ThingsBoard releases? I want to build against a stable target rather than something that will shift mid-GSoC.

**2. Attribute storage approach**
The current design uses a separate `entity_attributes` table with the same multi-typed-column pattern as telemetry, but with no time partitioning. Is there a preference from the ThingsBoard side on how attribute storage should differ from telemetry? For example, should attributes be modeled differently to support the `findAll` / `find` / `save` / `delete` operations the `AttributeDao` interface requires?

**3. Appetite for a new `database.ts.type` backend**
The path I have in mind is: land the module in `iotdb-extras`, demonstrate correctness with integration tests, then submit a PR adding `database.ts.type=iotdb-table` to ThingsBoard's DAO layer. Is the ThingsBoard team open to reviewing such a PR? Understanding the bar for acceptance early would let me design the integration and test suite to meet it from the start.

---

Any feedback on the schema, the attribute storage design, or the interface questions would be very helpful. Happy to share more detail on any part of this.

Thanks for your time,
Zihan Dai

nodes.title: AI-SPM v1.0.0 — AI Security Posture Management
nodes.body:
# AI-SPM v1.0.0 — AI Security Posture Management **Release date:** 2026-04-25 **Codename:** "MCP" > First production release of the AI Security Posture Management. Customers > can now upload their own AI agents as a single Python file, deploy > them into sandboxed containers, and have them chat through the full > security pipeline — prompt-guard → policy decider → Kafka → output-guard > — with attached policies, conversation memory, web search, and a live > activity timeline visible in the admin UI. --- ## Highlights - **End-to-end agent chat** through the existing AI-SPM security pipeline, with attached per-agent policies enforced on every turn. - **Drop-in agent uploads.** Operator drops in a single `agent.py`, the platform validates it, mints per-agent tokens, spawns a sandboxed Docker container, and routes traffic through Kafka. No custom image required for the five example agent shapes we ship. - **Provider-agnostic LLM proxy.** Native dispatch for Anthropic and Ollama (both OpenAI-compatible and native modes); operators switch providers in the UI without restarts or code changes. - **Live observability.** Every chat turn, web-search call, and LLM call emits a lineage event that lands in `session_events` and tails in the per-agent **Activity** tab in the admin UI within 5 seconds. - **DB-backed configuration.** The agent SDK fetches its connection bundle from the controller at boot — no platform secrets in the agent's container env. --- ## What's new ### Agent runtime control plane - **`POST /api/spm/agents`** — upload `agent.py` (multipart) with `deploy_after=true`. Validates syntax, top-level `async def main`, and dry-import; mints per-agent `mcp_token` + `llm_api_key`; creates the per-agent Kafka topics; spawns the runtime container; polls for the SDK's `aispm.ready()` handshake. - **`POST /api/spm/agents/{id}/start | /stop`** — idempotent kick; UI surfaces a persistent "working…" spinner until the polled `runtime_state` actually changes. - **`DELETE /api/spm/agents/{id}`** — stops the container, drops the topics, deletes the row. - **`POST /api/spm/agents/{id}/chat`** — full pipeline, SSE response. - **`GET /api/spm/agents/{id}/bootstrap`** — DB-backed SDK boot. The agent's container only needs three env vars (`AGENT_ID`, `MCP_TOKEN`, `CONTROLLER_URL`); everything else is fetched here. - **`GET /api/spm/agents/{id}/policies`** + **`PUT`** — atomic-replace attach/detach. The chat handler reads `linked_policies` per turn and forwards them to OPA so policies can scope evaluation. - **`GET /api/spm/agents/{id}/activity`** — unified timeline (chat turns + `AgentToolCall` + `AgentLLMCall`), newest-first, capped at 200 rows. Polled by the Activity tab. ### Agent-side SDK (`agent_runtime/aispm`) - `aispm.ready()` — lifecycle handshake. - `aispm.chat.subscribe()` / `reply()` — Kafka I/O. Consumer uses `auto_offset_reset="earliest"` so the very first message after deploy is never silently dropped during consumer-group join. - `aispm.chat.history(session_id, limit)` — replay persisted turns; example agents use this for conversation memory across turns. - `aispm.mcp.call("web_fetch", ...)` — JSON-RPC over HTTP to the MCP server; `web_fetch` is Tavily-backed. - `aispm.llm.complete(messages=, model=…)` — OpenAI-compatible call through `spm-llm-proxy`; the SDK no longer pins a default model so the operator's chosen provider model wins. - `aispm.get_secret(name)` — per-agent secret store. - `aispm.log("step", trace=…)` — structured lineage line on stdout. ### Provider dispatch (spm-llm-proxy) | `connector_type` | Endpoint | Auth header | Model source | |------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `anthropic` | `{base_url}/v1/messages` | `x-api-key` + `anthropic-version: 2023-06-01` | integration `model` (payload `model` honoured only when it starts with `claude`) | | `ollama` (`/v1`) | `{base_url}/chat/completions` (OpenAI-compatible) | none | payload `model` > integration `model` > `llama3.1:8b` fallback | | `ollama` (other) | `{base_url}/api/chat` (native) | none | payload `model` > integration `model` > `llama3.1:8b` fallback | Switching provider is a UI dropdown change on the **AI-SPM Agent Runtime Control Plane (MCP)** integration row — no restart, no agent re-deploy. ### Observability (`AgentToolCallEvent`, `AgentLLMCallEvent`) - `spm-mcp` emits `AgentToolCallEvent` after every `web_fetch`, capturing tool name, args, ok/error, and `duration_ms`. - `spm-llm-proxy` emits `AgentLLMCallEvent` after every chat-completion call (Anthropic and Ollama paths), capturing model, prompt and completion token counts, and ok/error. - Both events publish to `cpm.global.lineage_events`. The existing `lineage_consumer` persists them into `session_events` automatically. - Best-effort by design: a producer init failure never blocks the serving path. A `lineage_producer.send failed` warning is the only signal when Kafka is unreachable; chat keeps working. ### Admin UI - **Inventory → Agents tab** lists live agents alongside mock rows with a runtime-state pip and risk tint. - **PreviewPanel** (right-side panel on row click) carries the Run/Stop toggle, **Open Chat**, **View Detail**, and **Delete asset** actions. - **AgentChatPanel** (300px inline panel) opens from PreviewPanel's Open Chat. Composer pinned to bottom (`min-h-0` + `max-h(100vh-120px)` so it can never be pushed off-screen by long chat history). - **AgentDetailDrawer** (560px overlay) opens from PreviewPanel's **View Detail** button. Five tabs: Overview, Configure, Activity (live tail, polls every 5s), Sessions, Lineage. - **PolicySelector** lets operators attach/detach policies on a live agent without leaving the panel. - **Add Integration** modal: `enum_integration` fields render as real dropdowns of existing integrations (no more pasting UUIDs). - **Run/Stop button** stays in a "working…" state until the next poll observes the actual runtime-state change. ### Examples A new top-level [`Example agents/`](Example%20agents/) folder ships five ready-to-deploy agents — one per `agent_type` enum value: | File | `agent_type` | Demonstrates | |-------------------------------|---------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `custom_agent.py` | `custom` | Bare-SDK happy path with `aispm.chat.history()` conversation memory and a strong web-search prompt. | | `langchain_agent.py` | `langchain` | Off-the-shelf LangChain `AgentExecutor` + `@tool` calling our MCP / LLM proxies. | | `llamaindex_agent.py` | `llamaindex` | LlamaIndex chat-engine routed through `aispm.llm`, with a hand-rolled retrieval fallback. | | `autogpt_agent.py` | `autogpt` | Self-prompting plan → execute → reflect loop, capped at 3 hops. | | `openai_assistant_agent.py` | `openai_assistant` | OpenAI Assistants-style request shape (system + user + tools), no framework. | The runtime image now has `langchain==0.3.*`, `langchain-openai==0.2.*`, `llama-index-core==0.11.*`, and `llama-index-llms-openai-like==0.2.*` baked in, so `langchain_agent.py` and `llamaindex_agent.py` deploy cleanly without bringing your own image. --- ## Bug fixes - **`paused` agent immediately after deploy.** The upload route's `_wait_for_ready` was reading a stale identity-mapped Agent row from its own SQLAlchemy session and timing out, then overwriting the (correctly running) row to `crashed`. Fixed with `db.expire_all()` on every poll iteration. - **First message after deploy silently dropped.** The agent's Kafka consumer joined the group with the default `auto_offset_reset= "latest"`, so any message produced between `aispm.ready()` flipping the row to `running` and the consumer registering with the broker was skipped. Fixed by switching to `earliest`. - **`Prompt blocked by safety guard. (S2)` on the literal word "yes".** Three different code sites (two adapters and one module-level function injected via `guard_fn=`) had the same anti-pattern that forced `verdict=block` whenever any S1–S15 category appeared, even when the guard's own verdict was `allow`. Replaced with a length-based bypass for inputs under `GUARD_MIN_TEXT_LEN=8` chars and a score-threshold (`GUARD_BLOCK_SCORE=0.6`) gate on the category-escalation path. - **502 `Load failed` on chat.** The `agent_chat.py` SSE handler was importing `aiokafka` lazily but the package wasn't in `spm-api`'s requirements. Added the dep. - **500 `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'services.spm_api'`** in both `spm-llm-proxy` and `spm-mcp`. Both fell back to a brittle cross-service import. Inlined `_decode_secret` and dropped the cross-service registry lookup so each service is self-contained. - **`POST /v1/chat/completions` returning 500.** The proxy was hardcoded to Ollama's `/api/chat` shape; pointing **Default LLM** at Anthropic produced a 404 from `api.anthropic.com`. Now branches on `connector_type` and translates request + response shape per provider. - **`web_fetch` 404 on `http://spm-mcp:8500/mcp`.** The MCP server registered tools with FastMCP but never mounted FastMCP's HTTP transport. Added an explicit `POST /mcp` JSON-RPC handler. - **`spm-mcp` crashing at startup with `TypeError: issubclass() arg 1 must be a class`.** `from __future__ import annotations` in `tools/web_fetch.py` made FastMCP's annotation introspection blow up. Removed. - **`agents.code_blob` self-heal.** Operators who `rm`'d the bind-mount source previously broke the agent permanently. The runtime image now rewrites the file from `agents.code_blob` (DB-stored agent.py source) on every spawn. - **`Integrations` page blank after creating the agent-runtime row.** `OwnerAvatar` crashed with `Cannot read properties of null (reading 'split')` when the new row had no owner. Defensive null-name guard. - **`null is not an object (evaluating 'n.id')` UI crash.** The `mergeAgents` / `mergedAllAssets` / `adaptLiveAgent` chain had no null filtering, so a poll race during a failing fetch could leave a null entry in the array. All three layers now filter falsy entries. - **Pasting UUIDs into agent-runtime config fields.** `SchemaForm` didn't handle `type: "enum_integration"` and fell back to a text input. Now renders a dropdown of existing integrations filtered by the connector's declared `options_provider`. - **`AgentChatPanel` composer pushed below the fold.** Missing `min-h-0` on the flex column meant the message list grew unbounded. --- ## Operator changes - **New integration to configure on first install:** *AI-SPM Agent Runtime Control Plane (MCP)*, under Integrations → AI Providers. Set its **Default LLM** field to your existing AI Provider integration (e.g. Anthropic, Ollama) and **Tavily Integration** to your Tavily row. The proxy and MCP server resolve through this row at every call, so changing the upstream provider is a UI dropdown change with no restart. - **Runtime image rebuild required** to pick up the new framework batteries: ```bash docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.auth.yml \ --profile build-only build --no-cache agent-runtime-build ``` Adds ~200 MB to the image (LangChain + LlamaIndex). Existing agent containers should be force-removed before the next deploy: ```bash docker ps -a --filter 'name=agent-' -q | xargs -r docker rm -f ``` - **New env-var knobs** (all have safe defaults): | Variable | Service | Default | Purpose | |---|---|---|---| | `GUARD_BLOCK_SCORE` | `api`, `spm-api` | `0.6` | Min guard score to escalate `allow + category` to `block`. | | `GUARD_MIN_TEXT_LEN` | `api`, `spm-api` | `8` | Inputs shorter than this skip the guard entirely. | | `AGENT_READY_TIMEOUT_S` | `spm-api` | `30` | Deploy poll budget for the SDK's `ready()` handshake. | | `AGENT_CHAT_REPLY_TIMEOUT_S` | `spm-api` | `120` | How long the chat round-trip waits for an agent reply on `chat.out`. | | `AGENT_CONTROLLER_URL` | `spm-api` | `http://spm-api:8092` | What gets injected as `CONTROLLER_URL` into spawned agent containers. | | `KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS` | `spm-mcp`, `spm-llm-proxy` | `kafka-broker:9092` | Lineage producer bootstrap. | --- ## Database migrations Three new alembic revisions auto-apply on `spm-api` startup: - `005_agent_runtime_control_plane` — `agents`, `agent_chat_sessions`, `agent_chat_messages` tables; `agent_type` enum. - `006_agent_policies` — join table `agent_policies(agent_id, policy_id, attached_at, attached_by)` with cascade-on-agent-delete. - `007_agent_code_blob` — adds `agents.code_blob TEXT` so the runtime can self-heal a deleted host file. All migrations are forward-only; no data loss on upgrade. `005` is idempotent against duplicate-enum-create errors so re-applying is safe. --- ## Tests - **514 unit + integration tests** green (Python). - **3 e2e smoke tests** in `tests/e2e/` (skip cleanly without docker-compose; run when the stack is up). - New `TestChatWithPolicySmoke` covers the full Phase 4 path: register agent → wait for running → attach policy → POST `/chat` SSE → assert reply text + activity timeline contains both user and agent turns → detach policy → delete. --- ## Documentation - New top-level [`README.md`](README.md) sections: **Deploying an agent**, **Adding a new integration (LLM, Tavily, etc.)**, **Adding an LLM specifically — minimum setup**, **Adding a new asset type**. - [`docs/agents/operator-quickstart.md`](docs/agents/operator-quickstart.md) extended with the Phase 4 end-to-end flow diagram, bring-up checklist, provider dispatch table, gotchas table, and env-knob reference. - [`Example agents/README.md`](Example%20agents/README.md) covers the five example agents, what each demonstrates, what's baked into the runtime image, and how to read the Activity tab for debugging. - Plan documents committed for each phase under `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-04-25-agent-runtime-control-plane-phase-{1..4}-*.md`. - Design spec at `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-04-25-agent-runtime-control-plane-mcp-design.md`. --- ## Upgrade notes For an existing AI-SPM stack, this is a backwards-compatible feature release — no breaking changes to existing connectors, policies, or chat behaviour. To get the new agent runtime online: ```bash git pull docker compose build --no-cache spm-api spm-mcp spm-llm-proxy ui # Runtime image (LangChain + LlamaIndex baked) docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.auth.yml \ --profile build-only build --no-cache agent-runtime-build # Recreate docker compose up -d --force-recreate spm-api spm-mcp spm-llm-proxy ui # Stop any stale agent containers (they have the old env contract) docker ps -a --filter 'name=agent-' -q | xargs -r docker rm -f ``` Then in the UI: 1. Configure an LLM provider integration (Anthropic / Ollama / etc.). 2. Configure the **AI-SPM Agent Runtime Control Plane (MCP)** integration; pick the LLM provider and Tavily on it. 3. Inventory → Agents → Register Asset → drop in [`Example agents/custom_agent.py`](Example%20agents/custom_agent.py) → type `custom` → Register & Deploy. 4. Open Chat. Send a message. --- ## Known limitations - **Per-agent `requirements.txt`** isn't supported yet; agents that need packages outside the baked-in set (LangChain, LlamaIndex, the SDK transport deps) require forking the runtime Dockerfile. Planned for V2. - **`AgentDeployedEvent` / `AgentStartedEvent` / `AgentStoppedEvent`** dataclasses exist in `platform_shared/lineage_events.py` but aren't yet emitted from `agent_controller`. Only `AgentChatMessageEvent`, `AgentToolCallEvent`, and `AgentLLMCallEvent` flow through `lineage_consumer` today. - **Streaming token responses (`aispm.chat.stream`)** is a stub that raises `NotImplementedError` on `write()`. The SSE shape supports per-token frames, but the agent → Kafka path is one-message-per-reply. Planned for V1.5. - **Multi-tenant enforcement** on agent rows is on a single boundary (the list endpoint scopes by `tenant_id`); other surfaces are effectively single-tenant. V2 enforces strict isolation everywhere. - **Plaintext `mcp_token` / `llm_api_key`** at rest. The columns are admin-only and never returned in API responses, but V2 will encrypt with the existing Fernet key. - **OPA policy DSL** for agent-runtime context is a thin wrapper over the existing `spm/prompt/allow` and `spm/output/allow` rules; rules that reference `input.linked_policies` need to be authored. --- ## What's next (V1.1 / V2 roadmap candidates) - Per-agent `requirements.txt` builds. - `AgentLifecycle*` event emission from `agent_controller`. - Per-token SSE streaming through the chat pipeline. - Multi-tenant enforcement on every agent surface. - Encrypted-at-rest agent tokens. - Streaming Activity tab (SSE instead of 5s polling). - More built-in MCP tools beyond `web_fetch`. --- ## Acknowledgements This release was built end-to-end across Phase 1 (backend), Phase 2 (SDK), Phase 3 (UI), Phase 4 (chat pipeline), and Phase 4.5 (observability) over a single working day, against a live AI-SPM stack with iterative feedback at each step. Thanks to the operators who hammered the chat with `yes` until the guard-model false positive surfaced.
This discussion was created from the release AI-SPM v1.0.0 — AI Security Posture Management.
